collection.purpose: Source content for a set of gallery wall panels/posters. Each panel object below maps to one physical poster; the display pulls title, description, body, images and sources from its record.
collection.researchMethod: Web research via Tavily (search + image retrieval), June 2026.
curatorialNotes: Dating is reported inconsistently across sources: Wikipedia/UNESCO frame the Bura culture as 'first-millennium'; Grokipedia and several galleries give 3rd–13th c. CE; the Mulvane Art Museum cites 2nd–11th c. CE from stratigraphy. Panels use 'c. 3rd–13th century CE' with a note, and should be finalised against a primary source (Gado 1993).

Discovery: accidentally found 1975 (terracotta head[s]) near Bura-Asinda-Sikka; reported to IRSH, University of Niamey; first small dig 1978; first systematic excavation 1983 led by Boubé Gado. Some sources name the finder as villager Abdurahman Sindy.

Coordinates differ by source. Wikipedia gives 13°53′53″N 1°02′20″E (13.898, 1.039); Grokipedia gives ~13°50′N 0°30′E. Use the Wikipedia value as primary and verify against Niger heritage records before printing a precise pin.
collection.imageLicensingPolicy: Image URLs are research references only. Museum/Wikimedia images may be reusable under CC/open-access terms (verify per item); auction-house and commercial-gallery images are NOT cleared for reproduction. Confirm rights/credit for every image before it is printed on a panel. Prefer open-access (Wikimedia Commons, museum open-access) or commission original illustrations for A/C/D.
collection.demoUsagePolicy: This panel set is assembled for an in-engine DEMONSTRATION, not for publication or printed distribution. Cleared visuals: the four Met 'Bura peoples' objects are Public Domain (CC0, Met Open Access) and are downloaded into ./assets for same-origin display — these are safe to show and reuse. Un-cleared visuals (auction/commercial/editorial photos, and the site map) are shown only as low-resolution references for the demo and carry a 'usageNote'; the renderer stamps those panels 'For demo purposes only — not for distribution'. Replace or clear every flagged image before any public, printed, or distributed use.

panels.name: site-location-geography
panels.title: A Bend in the Niger
panels.subtitle: Where the Bura culture buried its dead
panels.panelCaption: Bura-Asinda-Sikka sits on a terrace of the middle Niger River valley in south-west Niger.
panels.description: The Bura necropolis lies in the Tillabéri Region (Téra Department) of south-west Niger, in the middle Niger River valley about 120–150 km north-west of Niamey, near the Burkina Faso border. The main necropolis is roughly one kilometre across, set in a natural cirque framed by 10–20 m buttes. Abundant river-terrace clay fed a vast terracotta tradition; the type-site anchors a network of 800+ related sites strung along the valley.
panels.body: Bura is the type-site of the Bura culture and was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List on 26 May 2006. Field surveys describe an ensemble of sites spanning ~450 km across western Niger — from the Malian border to the meanders of the 'W' river bend — including necropoleis, altars and habitation zones.
keyFacts: Region: Tillabéri, Téra Department, south-west Niger
Setting: middle Niger River valley, floodplain terrace
Coordinates (primary): 13°53′53″N 1°02′20″E (verify before printing)
~120–150 km north-west of Niamey
Main necropolis ≈ 1 km diameter; type-site of 800+ related sites
UNESCO Tentative List, 26 May 2006

panels.name: excavation-history
panels.title: The Village of the Dead
panels.subtitle: Boubé Gado and the 1983 excavation
panels.panelCaption: Accidentally found in 1975; systematically excavated in 1983 by Nigerien archaeologist Boubé Gado.
panels.description: A terracotta head turned up by chance near Bura-Asinda-Sikka in 1975 and was reported to the Institute for Research in Human Sciences (IRSH) at the University of Niamey. After a small 1978 dig, Boubé Gado led the first systematic excavation in 1983, opening a 25 × 20 m area and revealing over 600 (≈630) funerary urns — naming the site a necropolis, 'un village des morts'.
panels.body: Gado published the foundational account in 1993 ("Un 'village des morts' à Bura en République du Niger") in the catalogue 'Vallées du Niger'. The work was modestly financed by the University of Niamey and the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Bura-Asinda exhibition toured France in the 1990s. The site has since suffered extensive looting — Le Monde reports ~90% of Niger's Bura sites damaged since 1994 — which is part of why documented excavation imagery matters.
keyFacts: 1975 — accidental discovery (terracotta head)
1978 — first small-scale dig (IRSH, Univ. Niamey)
1983 — systematic excavation by Boubé Gado, 25 × 20 m trench
≈630 funerary urns recovered
Foundational paper: Gado, B. (1993), 'Vallées du Niger'
Heavy looting since the 1990s (Le Monde: ~90% of sites damaged)

panels.name: ceramic-typology
panels.title: Forms of the Bura Potter
panels.subtitle: A field classification of vessels and figures
panels.panelCaption: From tubular urns to mounted horsemen — the main Bura ceramic forms.
panels.description: Bura terracottas range from tall tubular urns (70–80 cm) and round/semi-ovoid urns to vessels surmounted by stylized human heads, standing figures and equestrian riders, plus zoomorphic forms. Surfaces carry scarification (incised marks) and raised ridged designs thought to encode the deceased's identity — status, occupation or hairstyle. Bura is credited by UNESCO with some of the oldest equestrian clay statues in the Sahel.
panels.body: Intact human or equestrian figures are very rare; most survive as heads or fragments. The rider figures bear a loose resemblance to later Djenné pieces and point to the prestige of the horse as a status marker before Islamic influence. A typology chart should show: (1) tubular urn, (2) ovoid/spherical urn, (3) head-topped cap, (4) standing anthropomorphic figure, (5) equestrian figure, (6) zoomorphic vessel.
keyFacts: Tubular urns 70–80 cm tall; round/semi-ovoid urns
Caps/figures: stylized heads, standing figures, horsemen, animals
Decoration: scarification (incised) + raised ridged designs
Oldest equestrian clay statues in the Sahel (per UNESCO)
Intact figures extremely rare; mostly heads/fragments survive

panels.name: burial-context
panels.title: Sealed for the Afterlife
panels.subtitle: How a Bura grave was arranged
panels.panelCaption: Urns set into the earth, often inverted, capped with a face — a guardian for the dead.
panels.description: Bura ceramics are funerary objects. Urns were typically placed in tight clusters and frequently inverted over the burial; human skeletal remains lay roughly 1–1.5 m below. Vessels held bones (sometimes only a skull) plus grave goods — iron arrowheads, bracelets or rings, and quartzite beads. A secondary statuette — a face in the likeness of the deceased, or an animal effigy — was set in the opening to protect and guide the dead.
panels.body: Researchers read the spherical, sky-facing urns and the phallic/tubular forms as distinct rites, and interpret a skull placed inside a guardian urn as a companion (servant, spouse or kin) meant to accompany the principal burial. The artifact anchoring this gallery — a clay jar-top face — most likely functioned exactly here: as a container cap or grave marker.
keyFacts: Urns clustered and often inverted over the burial
Skeletal remains ≈ 1–1.5 m below the vessel
Contents: bones/skull + iron arrowheads, bracelets, rings, quartzite beads
Face/animal statuette set in the opening as a 'guardian'
Scarification designs may encode status, trade or hairstyle

images.caption: A Bura grave marker / vessel of the kind set over a burial — often inverted, capping the interred remains below.

panels.name: cultural-network
panels.title: A Corridor of Clay
panels.subtitle: Bura among West Africa's terracotta cultures
panels.panelCaption: Bura belongs to a 2,000-year West African tradition of figurative terracotta.
panels.description: Bura sits within a long arc of West African terracotta-producing cultures that may share roots in the earlier Nok tradition. Placed on a map and timeline, the nodes connect: Nok (Nigeria, c. 1500 BCE–200/500 CE), Jenne-Jeno (Mali), Koma (Ghana), Igbo-Ukwu and Ile-Ife (Nigeria), and Bura (Niger, c. 3rd–13th c. CE). Bura's valley would later give rise to the Songhai Empire.
panels.body: Nok is regarded as the earliest large figurative sculptural tradition in sub-Saharan Africa and an early centre of iron-smelting; scholars suggest later traditions — Bura among them — 'may have been shaped by' that ancestral clay tradition. The panel should make clear these are related but distinct cultures across different centuries, not a single lineage.
keyFacts: Nok (Nigeria): c. 1500 BCE – 200/500 CE — earliest figurative terracotta
Jenne-Jeno (Mali): urban centre, ~11th–12th c. CE terracottas
Koma (Ghana): c. 7th–15th c. CE
Igbo-Ukwu / Ile-Ife (Nigeria): 9th–15th c. CE
Bura (Niger): c. 3rd–13th c. CE
Shared themes: terracotta figures, ironworking, funerary ritual

panels.name: museum-holdings-provenance
panels.title: From Niger Soil to the Vitrine
panels.subtitle: Holdings, provenance and the ethics of collecting
panels.format: Text + institution panel with a provenance trail
panels.panelCaption: Where Bura objects are held today — and the looting that shadows them.
panels.description: Documented Bura terracottas are held by the Musée National du Niger (Niamey), the Musée du quai Branly–Jacques Chirac (Paris), the Smithsonian's National Museum of African Art (Washington DC, 2001 'Archéologie au Niger'), Yale University Art Gallery, and the Mulvane Art Museum, among others. Because ~90% of Bura sites have been looted since 1994, provenance matters: ICOM lists Bura funerary objects on its Red List of at-risk West African heritage.
panels.body: A provenance trail makes the journey legible. Yale's Bura anthropomorphic figure, for example, is recorded as: Wayne Cancro, Jersey City (1981–2004) → SusAnna and Joel B. Grae, New York (2004–2010) → Yale University Art Gallery (2010–). Pairing a clear chain of custody with the ICOM Red List turns the panel into a statement on responsible stewardship — and connects directly to the gallery's own Met relief.
keyFacts: Holdings: Musée National du Niger; quai Branly (Paris); Smithsonian NMAfA; Yale; Mulvane
Smithsonian show: 'Archéologie au Niger' (2001), Gado/Maga/Idé
ICOM Red List (West Africa) flags Bura funerary objects as at-risk
~90% of Niger's Bura sites looted/damaged since 1994 (Le Monde)
Example trail: Cancro → Grae → Yale University Art Gallery
